title: THE TIMEKEEPER
standing: An invented suspect. The history is real.

suspect.name: The Timekeeper
suspect.line: Wanted: for trying to wind the world back to 1788.
suspect.portrait_note: BK's Gemini illustration (22:11), placed by Josh with the prompt logged.
suspect.portrait_alt: An invented figure in silhouette, holding a pocket watch.
suspect.portrait_src: Illustration: Mr. Kelley, made with Google Gemini (AI).

intro: Someone is winding the clocks back.
The Timekeeper wants the world the way it was in 1788, before France's revolution carried new ideas across Europe and the world. Everywhere those ideas spread, he tried to stop the clock.
Follow his trail. Every place, date and document in this chase is real. He isn't.
At the end, you'll name an enduring issue three of his stops share, and prove it.

stops.story: In 1789, France's National Assembly writes down that men are born free and equal in rights. The Timekeeper arrives too late: the words are already printed.

clue.text: Open the Enduring Issues map: The Declaration of the Rights of Man.

ask.stem: According to the Enduring Issues map stop, law is supposed to be the expression of what? Type it.
hints: Read what happened at the map stop.
Look for the word law.

stops.evidence: 1789 · Article 2: liberty, property, security and resistance to oppression · Document 3 (Casefile B)
stops.after: You found it. Copy the evidence card into box 1.

stops.story: In 1791, the enslaved people of Saint-Domingue rise up against slavery. In 1804, Haiti declares its independence. The Timekeeper can't wind this clock back.

clue.text: Open the Enduring Issues map: The Haitian Revolution.

ask.stem: According to the Enduring Issues map stop, who declared Haiti independent in 1804? Type his last name.
hints: Read what happened at the map stop.
Look for the year 1804.

stops.evidence: 1793 · Toussaint calls his brothers to fight for Liberty and Equality · Document 1 (Casefile C)
stops.after: You found it. Copy the evidence card into box 2.

stops.story: In 1808, Napoleon puts his brother on Spain's throne, and Spain's colonies across the ocean must decide whether to obey a French king. The Timekeeper is one step behind.

clue.text: Open the Atlas: Central Europe in 1812. Look at the small map.

ask.stem: On the small map, which giant empire directly east of the Duchy of Warsaw stayed independent of Napoleon in 1812? Type its name.
hints: Find the color for independent states.
Look east of the Duchy of Warsaw.

stops.evidence: 1808 · Spain gets a French king, and its colonies soon take over their own governments · Document 3 (Casefile C)
stops.after: You found it. Copy the evidence card into box 3.

stops.story: Napoleon has been beaten. In Vienna, the winners redraw the map, and old ruling families take back their thrones. Every clock in the city reads 1788.

ask.stem: In 1815, who holds Lombardy and the city of Venice in northern Italy? Type the empire.
hints: Find northern Italy at the bottom of the map.
Lombardy and Venetia aren't filled in. Match the colored line along their border to the key.

stops.after: Austria takes back Lombardy and gets Venice too. The old Republic of Venice never comes back. The trail has gone cold. But you can't wind back an idea.

stops.story: In 1846, Camillo di Cavour, a nobleman from Piedmont, writes that Italians must silence the small questions that divide them. The idea the Timekeeper buried in Vienna is back: people who share a language and a history should rule themselves. That's nationalism.

clue.text: Open the Atlas: The Unification of Italy, 1815–1870.

ask.stem: Italy's unification starts in the Kingdom of Sardinia, ruled from Piedmont. Which city is its capital? Type it.
hints: Find Piedmont in the top left.
It's the city just left of the word Piedmont.

question.stem: Casefile C asks: What did more to build Italy and Germany: agreeing to unite, or “blood and iron”? Which sentence is the strongest thesis for Italy, using Document 5?
options: For Italy, agreeing to unite did more, because Cavour argued that Italians had to silence the petty questions that divide them.
Cavour wanted Italy to be glorious and powerful.
hints: A thesis answers the question, and someone could argue with it.
Which one picks a side?
question.why: The first answer picks a side and gives a reason; the other three only repeat Document 5. Strongest thesis doesn't mean the only answer: Italy also went to war in 1859, 1860, 1866 and 1870.

stops.evidence: 1846 · Cavour: silence what divides Italians · Document 5 (Casefile C)

stops.story: In 1862, Otto von Bismarck tells a committee of Prussia's parliament how Germany will be united.

clue.text: Open the Atlas: The Unification of Germany, 1815–1871. Look at the top map.

ask.stem: On the top map, which state's customs union (a trade group with no taxes at its borders) grows into the German Zollverein? Type the state's name.
hints: Read the first line of the top key.
Find Berlin.

question.stem: Document 6 (adapted) says the goal will be achieved “by blood and iron.” Which explanation best shows what that evidence means?
options: This shows he believed war and military strength, not democracy, would unify Germany.
This shows he wanted Germany to stay divided.
This shows he trusted voting to unite Germany.
This shows he planned to sell iron to other countries.
hints: What does he say will NOT reach the goal?
What could blood and iron stand for?
question.why: His actual words were “iron and blood,” and he meant war: Prussia fought Denmark, Austria and France, and in 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed.

stops.evidence: 1862 · Bismarck: blood and iron, not democracy · Document 6 (Casefile C)

stops.story: October 1912. The Balkan states are about to go to war with the Ottoman Empire, and Europe's great powers are trying to hold the lid on. The Timekeeper was here minutes ago.

clue.text: Open the Atlas: The peoples of Austria-Hungary, 1911.

ask.stem: According to the map, which people live in Bosnia? Type one of them.
hints: Find Bosnia in the south of the empire.
Match its color to the key: it's the fourth color down. The map spells Serbs “Servians.”

question.stem: Which enduring issue does Document 8 best show?
hints: What's about to boil over?
Open the Six Umbrellas card: why people fight.
question.why: A pot about to boil over, with the great powers holding the lid, is Conflict; six days later, the First Balkan War began.

stops.evidence: 1912 · BALKAN TROUBLES about to boil over · Document 8 (Casefile C)
stops.nearMiss: You just missed him. He left a map open on the table: the peoples of Austria-Hungary. Bosnia is circled.

warrant: 1 · Name the issue. Which enduring issue shows up at three of your stops? Use a name from the Six Umbrellas card.
2 · Set the scene. When and where? Use the first and last years of those three stops, and their places. Then say what people wanted.
3 · Explain it. What does it mean, and why is it a problem? Stuck? Open the Six Umbrellas card in the Arena. Read it, close it, then say it in your own words.
4 · Prove it. Pick one of your three stops. Who says or shows what? Then say how it shows the issue.
5 · Prove it again. Use another of your three stops.
6 · Once more, if you have time. On the test you'll need three documents.

final.prompt: Which enduring issue shows up at three of your stops? Type its name from the Six Umbrellas card.
hints: Look at your evidence cards. Which issue shows up at three of them?
Open the Six Umbrellas card for the issue's name.

after_by_answer.nationalism: That's it: Nationalism. You'll find it at stops 3, 5 and 6. Now write your case on your Case File, steps 1 to 6.
after_by_answer.conflict: That's it: Conflict. You'll find it at stops 2, 6 and 7. Now write your case on your Case File, steps 1 to 6.

wrong_feedback.identity and nationalism: That's the umbrella's title. Type the issue under it.
wrong_feedback.identity & nationalism: That's the umbrella's title. Type the issue under it.
wrong_feedback.unification: That's what happened. Which enduring issue drove it?
wrong_feedback.war: Close. What's its name on the card?

pill.label: Six Umbrellas card
pill.shows: the Six Umbrellas card with every issue's one-line definition (the Doc Assist pop-up, ruled 10/1)

final.callout: LEARN THE ENDURING ISSUES. On the Regents you name one yourself, with no list. Know these and you'll always have one ready. Practice anytime in the Arena: Enduring Issue, Level 1 (the matching game).

lines: He wound the clocks back at Vienna, and the idea came back anyway.
His trail ends in Sarajevo, in Bosnia. The Timekeeper is gone, and he never made history happen. People did.
On June 28, 1914, a Bosnian Serb nationalist shot the heir to Austria-Hungary's throne in Sarajevo.
A month later, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, and Europe went to war. That's World War I, in Unit 10.5.
You can't wind back an idea. You can only follow where it goes.
